ety.text: Adjective and noun from Middle English drye, dryge, drüȝe, from Old English drȳġe (“dry; parched, withered”), from Proto-West Germanic *drūgī, *draugī, from Proto-Germanic *drūgiz, *draugiz (“dry, hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerǵʰ- (“to strengthen; become hard”), from *dʰer- (“to hold, support”). The verb derives from Middle English drien, from Old English drȳġan (“to dry”), from Proto-West Germanic *drūgijan, from Proto-Germanic *drūgiz (“hard, desiccated, dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerǵʰ- (“strong, hard, solid”).

senses.d: Free from or lacking moisture.
ex: This towel's dry. Could you wet it and cover the chicken so it doesn't go dry as it cooks?
The weather, […] we […] both agreed, was too dry for the season.

senses.d: Unable to produce a liquid, as water, (petrochemistry) oil, or (agriculture) milk.
ex: This well is as dry as that cow.

senses.d: Built without or lacking mortar.
ex: [A]lready the gate was blocked with a wall of squared stones laid dry, but very thick and very high, across the opening.

senses.d: Anhydrous: free from or lacking water in any state, regardless of the presence of other liquids.
ex: Dry alcohol is 200 proof.

senses.d: Athirst, eager.
Free from or lacking alcohol or alcoholic beverages.
ex: Of course it's a dry house. He was an alcoholic but he's been dry for almost a year now.

senses.d: Describing an area where sales of alcoholic or strong alcoholic beverages are banned.
ex: You'll have to drive out of this dry county to find any liquor.

senses.d: Free from or lacking embellishment or sweetness, particularly
ex: These epistles will become less dry, more susceptible of ornament.

senses.d: Low in sugar; lacking sugar; unsweetened.
ex: Proper martinis are made with London dry gin and dry vermouth.

Fatima Blush: Oh, how reckless of me. I made you all wet.
James Bond: Yes, but my martini is still dry. My name is James.

senses.d: Amusing without showing amusement.
ex: Steven Wright has a deadpan delivery, Norm Macdonald has a dry sense of humor, and Oscar Wilde had a dry wit.

senses.d: The process by which something is dried.
ex: This towel is still damp: I think it needs another dry.

senses.d: A prohibitionist (of alcoholic beverages).
ex: The drys were as unhappy with the second part of the speech as the wets were with the first half.

senses.d: An area with little or no rain, or sheltered from it.
ex: Come under my umbrella and keep in the dry.

senses.d: The dry season.
ex: [T]he spring-fed river systems. Not the useless little tributary jutting off into a mud hole at the end of the Dry.

senses.d: An area of waterless country.
Unsweetened ginger ale; dry ginger.
ex: All day, all night you feel as if the Earth could fly/Three more all for fine Indian Gin and whiskey dry.
Can you buy dry ginger in Croatia? If not what is an alternative?

senses.d: A radical or hard-line Conservative; especially, one who supported the policies of British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s.
To lose moisture.
ex: The clothes dried on the line.
The fruit dried in the dehydrator.

senses.d: To remove moisture from.
ex: Devin dried her eyes with a handkerchief.
We dried the fruit in the dehydrator.

senses.d: To exhaust; to cause to run dry.
For an actor to forget their lines while performing.
ex: An actor never stumbled over his lines, he “fluffed”; he never forgot his dialogue, he “dried.”
In one of the previews I dried (lost my lines) in my opening scene, 1.4, and had to improvise.

grp.label: free of water in any state

ety.text: From Middle English driere, dreyere (“one who dries”), equivalent to dry + -er (agent noun suffix).

senses.d: One who, or that which, dries; any device or facility employed to remove water or humidity, e.g. a desiccative
ex: The sun and a northwesterly wind are great driers of the earth.

senses.d: A catalyst used to promote the drying of paints and varnishes by oxidative crosslinking.
